concepts.name: German sound-letter correspondences
concepts.summary: Understand how umlauts, ß, ch (ich/ach), sch, z, w, v and ei/ie map to sounds and read words aloud accurately.

concepts.name: Noun gender and articles
concepts.summary: Remember that every noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, learn nouns with their articles, and recall the plural article die.

concepts.name: Noun capitalisation and plurals
concepts.summary: Understand that all nouns are capitalised and recognise the main plural patterns (-e, -n, -er, umlaut, -s).

concepts.name: Present tense of sein and haben
concepts.summary: Recall the irregular present forms of sein and haben for all persons.

concepts.name: Regular present-tense conjugation
concepts.summary: Understand how stem plus -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en marks person and number, including du/Sie formality.

concepts.name: Basic main-clause word order
concepts.summary: Understand that the conjugated verb sits in second position in simple statements and begins yes/no questions.

concepts.name: Nominative and accusative basics
concepts.summary: Understand that the subject is nominative and the direct object is accusative, with the masculine article changing from der to den.

misconceptions.text: German nouns only need a capital letter at the start of a sentence or when they are names.
The gender of a noun can be predicted from its meaning, so a girl must be feminine.
The ch in ich and in Buch is the same sound.

concepts.name: Dative case and its triggers
concepts.summary: Apply dative articles for indirect objects and after prepositions such as mit, nach, bei, von, zu, aus, seit and verbs like helfen.

concepts.name: Two-way prepositions
concepts.summary: Choose accusative for movement toward a place and dative for location with in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben and zwischen.

concepts.name: Modal verbs with infinitive
concepts.summary: Use können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen and mögen with the infinitive at the end of the clause.

concepts.name: Separable and inseparable verbs
concepts.summary: Apply the split of the prefix to the clause end in main clauses, as in anrufen, and recognise inseparable prefixes like be-, ver- and er-.

concepts.name: Perfekt formation
concepts.summary: Form the Perfekt with haben or sein plus the past participle, choosing the auxiliary and building ge- participles for regular, irregular and separable verbs.

concepts.name: Negation with nicht and kein
concepts.summary: Apply kein to negate nouns with indefinite or no article and nicht for verbs, adjectives and definite phrases, placing it correctly.

concepts.name: Possessive articles and personal pronouns
concepts.summary: Understand and use possessive articles and personal pronouns across nominative, accusative and dative.

concepts.name: Subordinating conjunctions and verb-final
concepts.summary: Apply verb-final word order in clauses introduced by weil, dass, wenn and ob.

misconceptions.text: Nicht ein and kein are interchangeable, so Ich habe nicht Geld is correct.
All verbs form the Perfekt with haben.
After weil the verb stays in second position as in a normal statement.

concepts.name: Adjective endings
concepts.summary: Select the correct adjective ending by combining case, gender, number and whether the article is definite, indefinite or absent.

concepts.name: Genitive case usage
concepts.summary: Use the genitive for possession and with prepositions like wegen, trotz, während and statt, and contrast it with von plus dative.

concepts.name: Präteritum versus Perfekt
concepts.summary: Analyse when Präteritum is preferred in writing and with sein, haben and modals, and when Perfekt suits spoken or conversational past reference.

concepts.name: Relative clauses and pronouns
concepts.summary: Build relative clauses where the pronoun takes gender and number from its antecedent and case from its role, with the verb final.

concepts.name: Reflexive verbs and pronouns
concepts.summary: Use reflexive verbs with accusative or dative reflexive pronouns and distinguish them from non-reflexive uses.

concepts.name: Infinitive clauses with zu
concepts.summary: Form infinitive clauses with zu, um...zu and ohne...zu, including the placement of zu with separable verbs.

concepts.name: Inversion and word order variation
concepts.summary: Analyse how fronting elements triggers verb-second inversion and how time, manner, place and pronoun order arrange middle-field elements.

concepts.name: Compound noun analysis
concepts.summary: Decompose compound nouns, determine gender from the last element and interpret linking elements like -s- and -n-.

misconceptions.text: Adjective endings are arbitrary and must simply be memorised word by word.
A relative pronoun takes its case from the noun it refers back to.
Präteritum and Perfekt are fully interchangeable in any context.

concepts.name: Konjunktiv II for hypotheticals
concepts.summary: Analyse and form Konjunktiv II and the würde-construction to express wishes, unreal conditions and polite requests.

concepts.name: Konjunktiv I and reported speech
concepts.summary: Analyse how Konjunktiv I reports speech neutrally and when Konjunktiv II substitutes for forms identical to the indicative.

concepts.name: Passive voice and alternatives
concepts.summary: Analyse Vorgangs- and Zustandspassiv, agent phrases, passive with modals and substitutes like man, sich lassen and sein+zu.

concepts.name: Verb-preposition and case government
concepts.summary: Analyse verbs, adjectives and nouns bound to particular prepositions and cases, including da- and wo- compounds.

concepts.name: Extended participial attributes
concepts.summary: Analyse nominal phrases that pack a participle and its complements before a noun, as typical in formal written German.

concepts.name: Modal particles and pragmatics
concepts.summary: Evaluate how particles like doch, ja, mal, eben and halt colour tone, and judge register differences between du and Sie, spoken and written.

concepts.name: Textual cohesion with connectors
concepts.summary: Evaluate the choice among adverbial and coordinating connectors such as deshalb, trotzdem, außerdem and obwohl for logical and word-order fit.

misconceptions.text: Konjunktiv II is only a polite form and cannot express unreal conditions.
Indirect speech simply requires Konjunktiv I in every case.
German passive always requires werden and cannot express a resulting state.

concepts.name: Register and style evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether a text's vocabulary, syntax and nominal style suit contexts such as bureaucratic, academic, journalistic or colloquial German.

concepts.name: Regional variation and standard norms
concepts.summary: Evaluate differences among German, Austrian and Swiss standard varieties and dialect influence, judging acceptability against norms.

concepts.name: Information structure and theme-rheme
concepts.summary: Evaluate how fronting, passive, and middle-field ordering shape emphasis and discourse flow beyond grammatical correctness.

concepts.name: Crafting nuanced argumentative prose
concepts.summary: Create coherent, well-structured argumentative or essayistic texts that combine subjunctives, nominalisation and connectors with precision.

concepts.name: Translation and equivalence judgments
concepts.summary: Create translations that preserve meaning and tone, resolving German-specific features like compounds, particles and long sentences.

concepts.name: Language change and contested usage
concepts.summary: Evaluate evolving usage such as the weil verb-second, dative replacing genitive and gender-inclusive forms against prescriptive and descriptive views.

concepts.name: Word formation and neologism
concepts.summary: Create new, idiomatic words using derivation, compounding and prefix-verb patterns, and justify their acceptability.

misconceptions.text: There is one correct standard German, and regional forms from Austria or Switzerland are simply errors.
Long, nominalised sentences are always better German style.
A correct translation maps each German word to a single English equivalent.
